deep.reconstruction:
WHAT THE TABLE IS. The page is a numerical table. The primes in the left half are 19,43,67,139,163,211,283,307, all congruent to 19 mod 24. The primes in the right half are 23,47,71,167,191,239,263,311, all congruent to 23 mod 24. The previous page has the same layout for primes congruent to 7 and 11 mod 24. So Gauss is covering every prime p ≡ 3 (mod 4), split by residue mod 24.

THE NUMBERED ROWS (my identification, verified for every column I recomputed). For each p, write F_k = floor(kp/24) for k = 1..12.
- Blocks 1 and 3 (rows 1-6, then 7-12) are exactly F_k. Example, p=19: 0,1,2,3,3,4 | 5,6,7,7,8,9. Example, p=43: 1,3,5,7,8,10 | 12,14,16,17,19,21.
- Blocks 2 and 4 are R_k, the number of quadratic residues of p among the integers 1..F_k, i.e. in the interval (0, kp/24).
- Example, p=19 (residues 1,4,5,6,7,9 up to 9): R = 0,1,1,1,1,2 | 3,4,5,5,5,6.
- Example, p=163: R = 3,5,8,13,14,20. This is the famous case where 2,3,5,7,11,13 are all non-residues.
- From these, the partial Legendre sums can be read off: S_k = sum_{0<n<kp/24} (n/p) = 2R_k - F_k.

THE ROWS a, b, c, d. These are the numbers of properly primitive classes per genus, in Gauss's sense (forms ax^2+2bxy+cy^2), for determinants -p, -2p, -3p and -6p. In modern terms:
- a = h(-4p). This is 3h(Q(sqrt(-p))) for p ≡ 3 mod 8 and h(Q(sqrt(-p))) for p ≡ 7 mod 8. There is one genus.
- b = h(-8p)/2. There are 2 genera.
- c = h(-12p)/4. There are 4 genera.
- d = h(-24p)/4. There are 4 genera.
- Checks: p=19 gives h(-152)=6, h(-228)=4, h(-456)=8, hence b,c,d = 3,1,2. p=23 gives h(-184)=4, h(-276)=8, h(-552)=8, hence 2,2,2.

THE PURPOSE. The rows a-d are compared with interval sums of the Legendre symbol. Recomputing from Gauss's own rows, the following identities hold in every column I checked. That is all eight left columns for a, b, c, d, and all eight right columns.
- (A) a = S_12 = sum_{0<n<p/2} (n/p).
- (B) b = S_9 - S_3 = sum_{p/8<n<3p/8} (n/p). That is, h(-8p) = 2*sum_{p/8<n<3p/8} (n/p).
- (C) c = S_10 - S_8 = sum_{p/3<n<5p/12} (n/p). That is, h(-12p) = 4*sum.
- (D) d = (1/2)[(S_7 - S_5) + (S_11 - S_1)] = (1/2)[sum_{5p/24<n<7p/24} + sum_{p/24<n<11p/24}] (n/p).
  - For p ≡ 19 mod 24 the two pieces are equal, so d = S_7 - S_5.
  - In the right half, Gauss put vertical bars at rows 1 and 5 of block 2 and rows 7 and 11 of block 4. These are exactly the four interval endpoints used in (D).

So the page is an empirical, and probably confirmatory, test of formulas expressing the class numbers of determinants -p, -2p, -3p, -6p (p ≡ 3 mod 4) by excesses of residues over non-residues in subintervals of length p/24. The next page continues with mean values of class numbers (alpha + b log n, separated by odd and even determinants).
errors: No arithmetic errors found in the entries I recomputed. These were all F_k rows for 211, 263, 283, 307 and 311; R_k rows for 19, 23, 43, 67, 139 and 163; and the full a-d consistency checks for all 16 primes.

Several entries are visibly overwritten in bolder ink. Examples are 51 (307, row 4), 14 (163, row 5), 13 and 9 (139), 75 (283, row 12), and 10, 11, 11, 12 (43, last block), plus several on the right. The corrected values are the correct ones.

results.what: Class number of determinant -p (p ≡ 3 mod 4) equals the excess of residues over non-residues in (0,p/2).
results.modern_name: Dirichlet class number formula, finite form: h(-4p) = sum_{n<p/2}(n/p)
results.usually_credited_to: Dirichlet 1839; also stated in Gauss's posthumous Nachlass

results.modern_name: Interval (Lerch/Berndt-type) class number formula for Q(sqrt(-2p))
results.usually_credited_to: Dirichlet/Lerch (1897-1905), Holden, Karpinski; surveyed by Berndt 1976

results.modern_name: Class number of Q(sqrt(-3p)) via Legendre sums over twelfths
Class number of Q(sqrt(-6p)) via Legendre sums over 24ths

results.what: Tables of floor(kp/24) and of residue counts in (0,kp/24).
results.modern_name: Partial character sums of the Legendre symbol

deep.surprise_reason: It is known that Gauss's Nachlass (e.g. De nexu inter multitudinem classium) relates class numbers to residue counts, so formula (A) is his. The systematic 24th-interval formulas for determinants -2p, -3p, -6p, with the correct interval combinations flagged, are usually associated with Lerch, Holden and Berndt-era literature. Clear evidence that Gauss had them empirically, or knew them, would be a notable unpublished detail. However, the page is a table, not a proof, and parts may be implicit in published Nachlass material.

checkable.asserts: Row a equals sum_{n<p/2}(n/p) for all 16 primes.
Row b equals sum over (p/8,3p/8) of (n/p).
Row c equals sum over (p/3,5p/12) of (n/p).
Row d equals half the sum of the (5p/24,7p/24) and (p/24,11p/24) Legendre sums.
Blocks 2 and 4 are residue counts in (0,kp/24) (example p=163).

transcription_corrections: The machine transcription matches the image for all entries checked. The bold overwritten digits (e.g. 51, 14, 13, 9, 75 on the left; 14, 19, 26, 36, 5, 6, 7, 38, 47, 57, 67 on the right) are the final corrected values and are correctly read.

The vertical bars in the right half mark rows 1, 4, 5 (block 1), rows 1, 5 (block 2), and rows 7, 11 (block 4), plus bold labels 9, 10, 11, 12 in block 3. These are the interval endpoints Gauss needed. The transcription renders every row with '|', which loses this distinction.
